topic: Theoretical Model of a Thermochemical Metal Oxide Cycle for Hydrogen Production
title: Theoretical Model of a Thermochemical Metal Oxide Cycle for Hydrogen Production
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Computing and Process Control
authors_text: Rachel Viger, Janna Martinek and Alan W Weimber
abstract: This work presents a three-dimensional, transient computational model for a two-step thermochemical hercynite water splitting cycle that is developed to optimize the design and operating conditions of a 4kW multiple tube solar receiver. A ray-tracing model is applied to determine the magnitude and direction of the concentrated, incident solar radiation on the aperture. The spectral and directional optical properties are applied to a Monte Carlo ray-tracing model that determines the transport of the solar radiation within the cavity. The emitted radiative transfer is calculated using a Radiosity model, which is coupled to heat transfer, species transport, and chemical reaction kinetics in a computational fluid dynamics model. The absorbing cavity contains an array of reaction tubes, each with an inner porous medium of cobalt ferrites deposited on alumina substrates that undergo a two-step water splitting redox cycle to produce hydrogen. The simulation results examine material properties, geometries, operating conditions, cycle time, and solar profile shape, and the trends in aperture size, number of tubes, and amount of reaction material are further assessed. Performance is improved with a large number of small-diameter tubes; however, the tube placement within the cavity has minimal impact. Configurations for both isothermal and temperature swing operation are analyzed, and indicate that similar time-averaged solar-to-chemical efficiencies, accounting for O 2 separation and steam vaporization, of up to 14% are achievable.

topic: Converged Free Energies of Binding in Cucurbit[7]Uril and Octa-Acid Host Systems from Expanded Ensemble Simulations
title: Converged Free Energies of Binding in Cucurbit[7]Uril and Octa-Acid Host Systems from Expanded Ensemble Simulations
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Computing and Process Control
authors_text: Jacob I. Monroe and Michael R. Shirts
abstract: Molecular containers, such as cucurbit[7]uril and the octa-acid cavitand host, have been used in a wide variety of applications, including selective drug delivery and release, specific molecular capture, and even for use in molecular machines such as nanoscale locks. Due to their ability to bind guests in a highly specific manner over a wide range of binding affinities, these small-molecule hosts are ideal test systems for optimizing and analyzing methods for computing free energies of binding that are also applicable to biologically relevant proteins. To this end, we have performed initially blind free energy calculations to determine the free energies of binding for ligands of both the cucurbit[7]uril and octa-acid hosts. A subset of the selected guest molecules were those included in the SAMPL4 prediction challenge, to which we made submissions for each host. For the expanded ensemble simulations that we have run, we are able to show that our estimates are converged and that the errors in our estimates are due only to the assigned force field parameters. This is confirmed through the use of alternative thermodynamic pathways, simulations of extended length, and analysis of sampled conformations. Our results also demonstrate the benefits of enhanced sampling of multiple local free energy minima imparted by the use of expanded ensemble molecular dynamics.

topic: Developing a System for Maintaining Ozone Levels in a Controlled Environment
title: Developing a System for Maintaining Ozone Levels in a Controlled Environment
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Computing and Process Control
authors_text: Andrew Fox, Dabrina Dutcher and Timothy Raymond
abstract: A method for monitoring and maintaining ozone levels in a reaction chamber was developed. Process control methods and a base software system were developed and calibrated. A user-friendly interface was also created. Previously, it has been difficult to maintain constant ozone levels in the reaction chamber and most experimentalists have simply added an initial amount of ozone that was depleted with time. While convenient and considered a standard technique in the field, this method is not representative of the ambient atmospheric environment. We used a PID control system that would be able to maintain the ozone levels both efficiently and in a timely manner. The software to maintain the ozone levels was developed in LabVIEW, a program using a visual programming language. With this program, appropriate software was developed that would take in external data from an ozone meter, record and interpret it, and translate it into a usable signal that would be sent to an ozone generator, which would finally correct the ozone level in the reaction chamber. The hardware system assembled consisted of the previously mentioned ozone meter measuring the current ozone level in the reaction chamber, a computer which was situated in the lab and ran the designed program, a DC conversion box which interpreted the signal from the software and converted into a usable DC current, a AC conversion box which converted the DC current to a AC current, and the abovementioned ozone generator, which was powered from the AC conversion box. The calibration of the system involved determining the appropriate constants to use for the PID control system, which were originally determined using the Ziegler-Nichols tuning method and then heuristically altered to better control the ozone levels. The user-interface was further developed to include a computerized recording and transcribing of the ozone levels in the chamber, an ozone purge mode where the program would deactivate until the ozone levels reached zero, at which point it would start up again, and a bypass mode where the user could selectively add ozone without the PID controller correcting the ozone level. The control system developed introduces an exciting new opportunity for the study of atmospheric chemistry. In real world environments, ozone levels, on average, remain relatively constant within a given biome. However, in prior research, ozone was left to deplete to zero during the course of an experiment. Utilizing the new system, ozone levels can be maintained at any desired level, just as it would be in any real environment. This will allow for more accurate interpretations and understandings of the reactions that are studied in the laboratory.

topic: 1-Dimensional PCA Approach for Classifying Imbalanced Data Sets
title: 1-Dimensional PCA Approach for Classifying Imbalanced Data Sets
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Computing and Process Control
abstract: Varayini Pankayatselvan, Derrick K Rollins, Sr. “1-Dimensional PCA approach for classifying imbalanced data sets” Major: Chemical Engineering The goal of data mining is to uncover patterns within large sets of data as to reveal important information. It is a subfield of several disciplines, including statistics and computer science. Imbalanced binary data sets pose a challenge in extracting information to produce high classification results. Some methods developed to classify these sets involve multi-parametric classification algorithms such as SMOTE, neural network and random forest. These methods can produce relatively high classification results, however their methodology can also be very involved. In bypassing the complexity, we have developed two powerfully simple one-dimensional classification methods producing high summary statistics. We implemented and modified a one-dimensional, PCA based approach, previously developed by Rollins et al., to separate imbalanced data sets on seven cases. Based on this PCA separation, we have developed two new classification techniques: mean method and spread method. In addition, we have also developed a feature reduction method in which we found an increase in classification results. We observed improved or similar results when comparing our data from the seven case studies with a recently published study on LVQ-SMOTE done by Kanazawa University in Ishikawa Japan. The summary statistics were sensitivity, specificity, and g-mean. We note that only providing these statistics do not give enough information on the validity of the classification technique. We challenge that the actual values for true positives and false positives should be provided.
authors: Varayini Pankayatselvan | NMSU, Las Cruces

topic: Technical Design, Implementation and Optimization of an Atomic Layer Deposition Reactor and Its Control System
title: Technical Design, Implementation and Optimization of an Atomic Layer Deposition Reactor and Its Control System
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Computing and Process Control
authors_text: Michael Schaefer, Mason A Chilmonczyk and Rudiger Schlaf
abstract: Technical Design, Implementation and Optimization of an Atomic Layer Deposition Reactor and its Control System Michael Schaefer 1 , Mason Chilmonczyk 2 , Rudy Schlaf 3 1 Department of Physics, University of South Florida, Tampa 2 Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of South Florida, Tampa 3 Department of Electrical Engineering, University of South Florida, Tampa Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) is a thin film manufacturing process that allows for angstrom thick layers to be uniformly placed on surfaces (including complex geometries) using self termination reactions via unique precursor gasses (e.g. Trimethylaluminum, Water, Titaniumtetracloride, Ammonia, etc.). Other methods such as Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD) do not guarantee a precisely controlled uniform surface coating due to an inability of controlling the reactions taking place. Our design is advantageous because of the capability of studying manufactured films and interfaces directly via x-ray photoemission spectroscopy (XPS), ultraviolet photoemission spectroscopy (UPS), and inverse photoemission spectroscopy (IPES). The combination of all three methods allows for a complete electronic structure analysis without taking the sample out of vacuum conditions, thus reducing the amount of surface contamination respectively surface oxidation under ambient conditions. This presentation covers the technical design and prototyping, control system, and implementation of the ALD reactor with an outlook on goals. The topics include: 1) Solidworks™ modeling and simulation, 2) Production and implementation of previously made designs, 3) Microcontroller usage (Arduino™, LabVIEW™) in an effort to control the necessary parameters like temperatures, pressures, injection timing, and carrier gas flow, 4) Printable circuit board (PCB) design (KiCAD™) and production based off of the prototyped setup, 5) Fabrication of a boxed control to ensure reliable use for an extended period of time, and 6) future optimization procedures and reaction control by studying the precursor injection behavior via differential pressure gauge readout.

topic: Investigation of Convex Methods in Optimal Power Flow
title: Investigation of Convex Methods in Optimal Power Flow
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Computing and Process Control
authors_text: David Ilavsky and Donald J. Chmielewski
abstract: This research looks at a new method of analyzing optimal power flow that should be easier and as accurate as current methods. Optimal power flow is the act of looking at how to minimize cost in generation of power by minimizing losses through a power grid. In the articles Convexification of Optimal Power Flow and Zero Duality Gap in Optimal Power Flow Problem by Lavaei and Low a new method is proposed for solving OPF problems. The accuracy and easy of the method will be analyzed by looking at 2 basic circuits which shall first be analyzed by current methods and then compared to the new convexification method analysis. The methods use for analysis will be DC analysis to provide a basis and then Gauss-Seidel analysis with the PowerWorld software to provide the accurate results. Finally the convexification method will be analyzed and compared to the results from the previous methods. The accuracy and easy of use of this new method would change how OPF problems can be solved and lead to better OPF solutions which would decrease power losses on the grid.

topic: Using Process Simulation to Estimate the Economics of Scaling up Experimental Results to an Industrial Scale
title: Using Process Simulation to Estimate the Economics of Scaling up Experimental Results to an Industrial Scale
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Computing and Process Control
abstract: Crude glycerin is obtained as a side product from the production of biodiesel. In its crude form, the glycerin has limited economic value. However, C3 compounds such as acrylic acid, acrolein, and hydroxyacetone which are traditionally derived from propylene can be produced from this crude glycerin. The purpose of this research is to determine if this glycerin dehydration process could be utilized on an industrial scale by using process simulation such as Aspen Plus. Results obtained from bench scale reaction experiments that convert glycerin into these chemical products will be integrated into Aspen which will in turn simulate this process on an industrial scale to see if this is an economically favorable process. This research has involved construction of a bench scale packed bed reactor, calibration of a gas chromatograph to analyze the results, and statistical design of experiments to optimize the process.

topic: The Modeling and Optimization of the Catalytic Hydrogenation of Butyric Acid to Butanol
title: The Modeling and Optimization of the Catalytic Hydrogenation of Butyric Acid to Butanol
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Computing and Process Control
authors_text: Keiron Durant, Jamie A. Hestekin and Thomas M. Potts
abstract: Butanol production has become an increasingly important process because of its direct impact on fuel cost savings and furthermore the economy. Using algae as a feedstock for butanol production has proven to be an effective method and consists of two main steps: fermentation of algae to form butyric acid and conversion of butyric acid to butanol. A catalytic hydrotreater is currently being used for the second part of the process and is executed by adding hydrogen to the butyric acid to make butanol. In order to make butyric acid for this process, algal solution that was formed from the hydrolysis of algae is left to react in a fermentation broth and then filtered. Carbon dioxide and hydrogen are both removed from the fermentation broth in this process. This research focuses on the optimization of the hydrogenation process i.e. the optimal operating conditions to achieve high butanol yield using plug flow reactor kinetics. The main reactions occurring during the hydrogenation are (i) conversion of butyric to butyric acid to butanol (desired reaction) and (ii) the conversion of butanol to butane (undesired reaction). This study investigates this problem by using reaction kinetics, mathematical modeling in Matlab® and Excel as well as process simulation in Aspen. The data fit the model best when the reaction was first order in butyric acid and zero order in hydrogen. Arrhenius activation energies, frequency factors were obtained and used to calculate equilibrium constants which were then compared to the experimental values. The data suggests that highest butanol yield occurs at and shorter residence times and that the reaction rate for the desired reaction increases with increasing temperature.

topic: Molecular Dynamics Simulations Highlight Structural Differences in Similar Intrinsically Disordered Protein Sequences
title: Molecular Dynamics Simulations Highlight Structural Differences in Similar Intrinsically Disordered Protein Sequences
session_title: Undergraduate Student Poster Session: Computing and Process Control
authors_text: Cayla M. Miller, G�l H. Zerze and Jeetain Mittal
abstract: Amylin, or Islet Amyloid Polypeptide (IAPP), a 37-residue polypeptide produced by beta cells, exists in vivo as an intrinsically disordered protein. The human form, hIAPP, has been implicated in the pathology of Type II Diabetes, where it forms toxic amyloid deposits, while the rat form, rIAPP, is nontoxic. hIAPP has proven to be difficult to study because of its rapid aggregation rate in vitro , so we have utilized molecular dynamics simulation in order to explore the structural properties of the monomer. We have compared the monomeric characteristics of hIAPP and rIAPP as well as two hIAPP mutants, I26P and S20G. Our results lead us to believe that differences in helicity over residues 7-16 may be a key factor influencing aggregation propensity. This is despite the fact that all four of these proteins have identical sequences over said region. Furthermore, we have found that previous studies of micelle-bound structures represent stabilized structures that are transiently sampled by monomers in solution.
